newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - Greenpeace ends Antwerp port soya protest.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Greenpeace ends Antwerp port soya protest.

text.p: Greenpeace activists on Friday ended a 24-hour blockade of a shipment of what they believed to be genetically altered soybeans in the Belgian Port of Antwerp.

Under a court injuction obtained by Cargill Benelux, a subsidiary of the U.S. grains multinational Cargill Inc which chartered the cargo, the activists would be fined a million Belgian francs ($32,000) for every hour the protest continued.
"Greenpeace is reluctantly ending (this) protest. But this is certainly not the end," James Gillies, a spokesman for the environmentalists' group, said.

The demonstrators had tied a rubber dinghy to the rudder of Polish registered bulk carrier Ziemia Zamojska to prevent it getting through one of Antwerp Port's four sea locks. Activists also chained themselves to the entrance to the lock.
The Antwerp Harbourmasters' Office said the action did not greatly affect traffic at Europe's second busiest port.
Greenpeace said the ship was carrying a new type of soybean developed by U.S. chemicals group Monsanto to be resistant to the company's own new "super weedkiller" Roundup.
Environmental groups describe the Roundup technology as a risky experiment with nature and a health risk.
But authorities in the United States and European Union say the new Monsanto strain poses no danger to the human food chain.
Greenpeace called on Cargill to segregate the soy and to reject further shipments of the genetically engineered beans.
A similar protest earlier this week in Hamburg, Germany, against what was believed to be the first genetic soy shipment ended peacefully after police intervened.
Amsterdam-based Greenpeace International has vowed to keep up a campaign of direct action against the imports.
Every week in Europe thousands of tonnes of soybeans are processed into meal and oil, which is used in a wide variety of everyday foods such as margarine, chocolate and mayonnaise.
Some leading European firms, including the German unit of Anglo-Dutch Unilever, have bowed to consumer pressure and announced they will not use the new variety even though they consider it safe.
Leading chocolate company Kraft Jacobs Suchard SA said on Friday it would not use the new soybeans in its European products for now, but was not opposed to the bean in principle on safety grounds.
